weather.typical: Maritime range catching heavy precipitation off Baker; can be wet/socked-in outside the summer window
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms/quick weather changes possible in late summer given proximity to Baker

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Real fall exposure on the steep dunite/olivine slabs; a slip on the slabs could mean a long, consequential fall, compounded by the remote, low-traffic setting where help is far away

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route; no NWAC forecast zone specifically covers this range/peak

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; route is dunite/olivine rock scrambling

fitnessSpec.hiking: Long, full approach-plus-summit day (likely 8-12+ miles round trip with significant elevation gain) over gated/rough logging roads and an informal ridge approach near Little Sister; extra road mileage on foot or bike if gates are locked
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light scrambling pack (roughly 15-25 lb) - helmet and light rack useful for the slabs; no glacier travel gear required

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - multi-hour approach via the Twin Sisters gated road network before gaining the southern ridge near Little Sister; a full-day objective, more if road gates add mileage
requiredSkills: unroped Class 3-4 scrambling on steep slabs
comfort with exposure on dunite/olivine slabs
navigating gated, seasonally-variable logging-road access on private/managed timberland
self-rescue readiness given remote, low-traffic terrain
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced scramblers only - comfortable with sustained unroped Class 3-4 travel, route-finding on an unmaintained approach, and self-sufficient remote travel; not a beginner objective

itinerary.cal: The Middle Fork Nooksack bridge/log crossing at the start of the Elbow Lake Trail washes out periodically - check recent trip reports before relying on a dry crossing.

days.note: Nearly all parties do this as a single long car-to-car day, not a backpack. Start by biking the washed-out lower Middle Fork Nooksack logging road to save the legs, then hike the Elbow Lake Trail up through old growth to the Sister Divide basin, before picking up climbers'-trail/cross-country ridge terrain on grippy olivine rock to Cinderella's summit. Descend by reversing the route, including re-biking the flat/downhill logging-road miles at the end.
days.title: Bike/hike approach and ridge scramble to the summit

schedule.label: Leave car, bike the logging road
schedule.detail: Lower Middle Fork Nooksack road/bridge access is washed out in sections; most parties bike the flat/rolling miles to save time and legs.

schedule.label: Stash bikes, start Elbow Lake Trail on foot
schedule.detail: Trail climbs steadily through old growth above Green Creek valley, about 4 mi / 3,000 ft to the Sister Divide highpoint area near Elbow Lake.

schedule.label: Reach Sister Divide / Elbow Lake basin
schedule.detail: Leave the maintained trail and pick up climbers'-trail and cross-country ridge terrain toward Cinderella.

schedule.label: Ridge/gully scramble to Cinderella summit
schedule.detail: Class 3-4 scrambling on solid, high-friction olivine rock; some exposed ridge sections and route-finding around gendarmes.

schedule.label: Reverse the scramble and hike back to bikes
schedule.detail: Downclimb the ridge, retrace the Elbow Lake Trail descent.

schedule.label: Bike out to the car
schedule.detail: Mostly downhill/flat logging-road miles back to the vehicle.

days.objective: Summit Cinderella Peak via the west ridge/Sister Divide olivine scramble, car-to-car

itinerary.totalNote: A long single push: roughly 11-12 hours car-to-car, ~12 miles and ~5,400 ft of gain, done in a day like nearly every party's report on this peak.

before.permit: No climbing permit; the approach crosses private and DNR timberland - check current access, and carry a Discover Pass where parking on DNR land.

access.fees: Day-use requires a Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent interagency pass; no separate climbing permit or fee for this unmaintained scramble route.
access.rules: Standard Wilderness-adjacent Leave No Trace ethics apply. The Green Creek climbers' trail is unofficial and unmaintained (blue flagging only) — stay on the existing boot path where possible, since the Twin Sisters' exposed olivine (dunite) supports a rare serpentine-adapted plant community.
access.permit: Northwest Forest Pass (or America the Beautiful/interagency annual pass) required to park at the Elbow Lake Trailhead; self-pay iron ranger at the trailhead, or purchase in advance at the Mt. Baker Ranger District office.
access.closures: Forest Road 38 has a seasonal closure gate at Wallace Creek, about 1.3 miles before the Elbow Lake Trailhead, typically shut roughly Dec 1-Jun 15 (exact dates vary by year/snowpack) — and FR 38 is separately closed at milepost 7 by a washout, per a Forest Service alert dated 27 July 2026, which blocks vehicle access to the trailhead entirely. Check MBS National Forest road status before driving. No gated logging-road network on the standard approach.
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mt. Baker Ranger District (810 SR-20, Sedro-Woolley, WA); the Twin Sisters peaks sit within/immediately adjacent to the Mount Baker Wilderness — not private industrial timberland.
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker Ranger District) — Mount Baker Wilderness, with some upper routes crossing into North Cascades National Park
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at most trailheads — $30/year or $5/day.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful Pass

overnight_permit.where: Camping is on unregulated Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and private timberland; no wilderness permit or registration is needed. The Dailey Prairie logging-road gate is separately locked to vehicles by the timber company, which is an access issue unrelated to camping.

waypoints.name: Elbow Lake Trailhead (FR-38)
waypoints.note: North end of Elbow Lake Trail #697 off Mosquito Lake Rd/FS-38, ~11 mi in; no bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack near here, so high flows can strand you at the car.
waypoints.directions: Take SR-542 from Bellingham through Deming to Mosquito Lake Road, then turn off onto FS-38 and follow it about 11 miles to the road end. It is gravel and normally in reasonable shape, but the lower Middle Fork Nooksack road has washed out in sections in the past and parties then bike the flat closed miles rather than walk them. Check the current road status before counting on driving to the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Elbow Lake
waypoints.note: Trail's namesake lake passed early on boggy ground among old-growth trees; last reliable easy water before the climbers' trail leaves the maintained tread.
waypoints.directions: The trail meets the Middle Fork Nooksack within a few minutes of the car and there is no bridge — it has been gone for decades, and any log that replaces it tends to wash out. The marked ford can be dangerous or impossible at high flow, so most parties use an unofficial crossing about a quarter mile downstream, logs lashed between two boulders. Once across, bushwhack the short distance back up to the Elbow Lake Trail proper and start climbing through old growth.

waypoints.name: Twin Sisters Viewpoint / Green Creek climbers' trail split
waypoints.note: First open view of the Twin Sisters Range near a switchback by Hildebrand Creek; the unofficial, sparsely-blazed Green Creek climbers' trail branches off the maintained tread here.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the maintained tread as it climbs above the Green Creek valley through old-growth forest, roughly a mile and a half from the crossing. Near 2,600 ft the trail swings into the Hildebrand Creek drainage, and it is at a switchback here that the unofficial Green Creek climbers' trail branches off. It is marked only by small blue markers on the trees — they are easy to walk straight past, so start looking for them before you think you need to.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Nooksack River crossing
waypoints.note: Climbers' trail drops back down to an unofficial log/logjam crossing of the Middle Fork Nooksack; no bridge, and it can be dangerous or impassable during high runoff.

waypoints.name: Little Sister saddle
waypoints.note: Col between Little Sister (6,600') and Cinderella Peak gained via boulder fields and scree above the Green Creek cirque; marks the start of Cinderella's west ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow the blue-blazed climbers' trail up into the Green Creek cirque; Green Creek runs clear and is the water source along this stretch. Above the trees the path gives out into talus, boulder fields and then loose, unstable scree, with Class 3 rock steps needed to reach the toe of the Green (Sisters) Glacier — route-finding through here is the crux of the approach and the least-loose line has to be hunted for rather than followed. Cross the low-angle glacier, carrying basic glacier gear, to the low notch on the ridge between Cinderella and Little Sister. Gain from the river to the notch runs to several thousand feet, which is why most parties break the trip up rather than pushing car-to-car.

waypoints.name: West ridge scramble section
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 exposed scrambling on the range's signature red olivine rock, which is grippy but the ridge narrows with real exposure; take care downclimbing if wet.
waypoints.directions: From the notch climb onto the blunt ridge crest above. The olivine here is exceptionally high-friction on the shaded north aspects and many parties solo it or run the rope, but the crest narrows and the exposure is genuine, and the same rock is far less secure when wet. Do not treat the connecting ridge back toward Little Sister as a traverse option — it is loose enough that the standard practice is to drop to the glacier from this notch instead.

waypoints.name: Cinderella Peak
waypoints.note: True summit at the west end of the Green Creek circuit; olivine rock underfoot is among the best scrambling texture in the Cascades.
waypoints.directions: The last Class 3-4 steps go on grippy dunite to the small summit block; where a step looks blank, working slightly left or right generally finds a passable line and nothing is sustained. Stay on the crest and the shaded aspects — south-facing rock in this range is markedly chossier and rocks pick up speed fast on it.

before.approach: Start at the Elbow Lake Trailhead (USFS Trail #697), at the end of FS Road 38 (the Mosquito Lake Road / FS-38 drive from Deming/Acme). The trail immediately meets the Middle Fork Nooksack River — there is no bridge at the marked crossing, and fording can be dangerous or outright impassable during high water; many parties instead use an unofficial log crossing roughly 1/4 mile downstream from the official ford, made of logs lashed between two boulders. Once across, pick up the Elbow Lake Trail proper and climb through forest for about 1.5 miles to a switchback near Hildebrand Creek, where an unmaintained but well-trodden, blue-blazed 'Green Creek Climber's Trail' splits off to the left into the Green Creek cirque (look closely for the small blue markers — it's easy to walk past). Follow this climber's trail up into the basin; Green Creek itself runs clear and is a reliable water source along this stretch. Above treeline the trail gives way to talus and boulder fields and then loose, unstable scree, with class 3 rock steps required to reach the toe of the Green Creek (Sisters) Glacier — route-finding through this section is the crux of the approach, and parties should expect to hunt for the least-loose line. Cross the low-angle glacier (crevasse hazard is generally low here but rises later season; carry basic glacier gear) up to the low notch on the ridge between Cinderella and Little Sister, which is the jumping-off point for Cinderella's west ridge/north face. Elevation gain from the river crossing to this notch is substantial — on the order of 4,500-5,500 ft over several miles — and most parties treat this as a multi-day trip, camping near Elbow Lake or in the Green Creek basin rather than going car-to-car.

approach_variants.name: Elbow Lake Trail and the Green Creek path to the low notch on the Cinderella-Little Sister ridge
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Elbow Lake Trailhead (Trail #697) at the end of FS Road 38. The trail immediately meets the Middle Fork Nooksack — there is no bridge at the marked crossing, and fording can be dangerous or impassable at high water. Many parties use an unofficial log crossing roughly a quarter mile downstream of the official ford, made of logs lashed between two boulders. Once across, climb through forest about 1.5 miles to a switchback near Hildebrand Creek, where the unmaintained, blue-blazed Green Creek Climber's Trail splits LEFT into the Green Creek cirque. Look closely for the small blue markers; it is easy to walk past. Follow it up into the basin — Green Creek runs clear and is a reliable water source along this stretch. Above treeline the trail gives way to talus and boulder fields and then loose, unstable scree, with Class 3 rock steps to reach the toe of the Green Creek (Sisters) Glacier. Route-finding through that section is the crux of the approach. Cross the low-angle glacier to the low notch on the ridge between Cinderella and Little Sister. Most parties treat this as a multi-day trip, camping near Elbow Lake or in the Green Creek basin.
hazards: A bridgeless Middle Fork Nooksack crossing, impassable at high water
An easy-to-miss blue-blazed junction near Hildebrand Creek
Loose unstable scree and Class 3 steps to reach the glacier — the crux of the approach
A moat at the glacier margin in both directions
A connecting ridge toward Little Sister that accounts describe as a missile zone
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LOW NOTCH ON THE CINDERELLA-LITTLE SISTER RIDGE IS THE BASE, AND IT IS WHERE YOU STOW GLACIER GEAR. Cross the low-angle Green Creek (Sisters) Glacier and step off ice onto rock at the notch. It is a col: a low point with a peak at each end of it, Cinderella one way and Little Sister the other.

THE MOAT AT THE GLACIER MARGIN IS THE LAST OBSTACLE AND IT IS SEASONAL, NOT STRUCTURAL — trivial in a heavy snow year, a real step late in the season, and exactly the same problem in reverse on the way down. Plan for it in both directions rather than being surprised at 4pm.

FROM THE NOTCH, GO WEST, NOT EAST. Cinderella's WEST RIDGE is the route — a long ridge, mostly straightforward walking on broken ground with a short section of enjoyable scrambling to the true summit. Turning the other way out of the notch heads for Little Sister.

DO NOT BE TEMPTED ALONG THE CREST TOWARD LITTLE SISTER. This is not mere caution: at least one party calls that connecting ridgeline a missile zone and recommends dropping back to the glacier from this notch instead of traversing it. The notch serves two peaks and connects neither.

ON THE WEST RIDGE, THE CREST DIRECT IS THE TRAP. Taking it absolutely direct runs into stretches of committing downclimbing; the standard escape is to DROP INTO A GULLY ON THE SOUTH SIDE and regain easier ground above. Committing downclimbing on a Class 3-4 scramble means you have stayed on the crest too long.

THE ROCK IS DUNITE AND IT BEHAVES TWO WAYS AT ONCE, which is the single most useful thing to know about holds here: notably grippy on WEATHERED surfaces, and greasy where a block has FRESHLY BROKEN. Judge each hold on its surface, not on the rock type.

before.beta: A short but rugged Twin Sisters Range outing combining glacier travel with class 3-4 scrambling on famously high-friction olivine rock. Most parties reach the peak as an overnight trip via the Green Creek cirque, either as a stand-alone objective or as part of the longer Green Creek Circuit traverse linking South Sister, Skookum, Little Sister, and Cinderella.

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman to the bench, then right around the buttress into the cleft
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is shared with Cosley-Houston, the Polish Route and Kimchi Suicide Volcano: from Glacier, WA up Glacier Creek Road (FS-39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, then Trail #677 onto the Coleman Glacier moraine and glacier travel climber's right to the bench beneath Colfax's north face.

What is different about this route begins at the bench rather than before it. Ford's Theatre is the RIGHTMOST of the four lines and it is about 500 ft of AI4+: three pitches of steep ice before the angle relents into steep snow gullies. Belay options after the first pitch are scarce, and the first-ascent party recommended running pitches two and three together to avoid hanging ice-screw belays.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr — the first ascent was 20 April 2015 and this is a cold-season ice line
hazards: Sustained AI4+ with almost no belay options after the first pitch
Hanging ice-screw belays if the pitches are not run together
The route is hidden from the approach, so its condition cannot be assessed before committing
Avalanche on this aspect after new snow, and the same overhanging bergschrund problem as the neighbouring lines
Crevasses on the Coleman and a glacier descent that should not be left until after dark
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IF YOU CAN SEE YOUR ROUTE FROM THE BENCH, IT IS NOT FORD'S THEATRE. That is the single most useful fact about this climb and it is the one the first-ascent party chose to record: most of the route is HIDDEN during the standard approach to the north face, because it sits in a cleft around the RIGHT side of a buttress. The other three lines are all visible from the approach. This one is not.

SO THE PROCEDURE IS: walk right along the base of the face, past the Cosley-Houston line, until a buttress cuts the face off from view — then go around the right side of that buttress. The route is in the cleft behind it. A climber who stops at the first steep ice they can see has stopped on Cosley-Houston.

LEFT TO RIGHT, THE FOUR LINES ARE: KIMCHI, POLISH, COSLEY-HOUSTON, FORD'S THEATRE. This is the far right end of that list, which is why the instruction is always 'keep going'.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: three pitches of sustained steep ice, roughly 500 ft, then the angle eases into snow gullies. Belays are hard to find after the first pitch. If you get a comfortable stance every rope length, or if the route stays steep for far more than 500 ft, you are on something else.

WHAT BEING SHORT LOOKS LIKE: Cosley-Houston starts with a LOW-ANGLE ICE RAMP above the schrund leading to a crux pillar. If you are walking up a ramp, you are one line to the left of where you meant to be — which is a fine route and a different one.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: April through June, with April-May generally offering the firmest, coldest conditions

May.reason: Continuation of the firm spring window; still within the April-June best-season range

July.reason: The couloirs melt out in summer, increasing rockfall

June.reason: Later in the window rockfall as the couloir warms becomes more pronounced, so timing/early starts matter more

April.reason: Firm alpine ice/snow on the Black Buttes couloirs as the prime season signature

March.reason: Couloir often not fully formed yet; deeper unconsolidated snow and less-predictable ice per climate data for this range

weather.typical: Cold, firm conditions in the prime spring window; approach and route sit on the west shoulder of Mount Baker and are exposed to typical Cascades maritime storm cycles between clear high-pressure windows
weather.probability: Warming through the day increases the rockfall hazard in the couloir, which is why an early 3-4 AM start is recommended; June ascents face higher probability of afternoon warmth accelerating rockfall

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High consequence: sustained steep ice above a bergschrund with a loose rock exit; a fall or rockfall strike in the couloir is serious given the remote setting and technical retreat

avalanche.zone: NWAC Mount Baker zone (covers the Black Buttes/Coleman Glacier approach)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Coleman Glacier approach involves roped glacier travel with crevasse hazard before reaching the bergschrund; the couloir itself is climbed above the bergschrund on ice/snow rather than open glacier

waypoints.name: Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Glacier Creek Road (FR 39), 8 mi from Hwy 542; Northwest Forest Pass required for parking, self-issue Mt. Baker Wilderness permit at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is at the end of Glacier Creek Road (Forest Road 39), about eight miles off Highway 542, at roughly 3,700 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and you self-issue a Mount Baker Wilderness permit at the kiosk there. Check current road status before you drive up, since conditions on FR-39 can vary.

waypoints.name: Kulshan Cabin site / creek crossings
waypoints.note: Established campsite at the old 1925 Kulshan Cabin site; bridged creeks along the lower trail provide reliable water before the climbers'-trail junction.

waypoints.name: Climbers' Trail / Hogsback Ridge junction
waypoints.note: Well-marked fork just past the Kulshan Cabin site: left continues to Heliotrope Ridge, right (climbers' path) climbs the Hogsback toward the Coleman Glacier.

waypoints.name: Hogsback Camp
waypoints.note: Camp sites scattered 6,000-6,200 ft along the moraine crest above the trees; standard bivy for Coleman Glacier and Colfax north-face routes.

waypoints.name: Coleman Glacier crevasse field
waypoints.note: Rope up crossing the glacier below Colfax; recent parties report a large crevasse forcing a lower, climber's-left detour.

waypoints.name: Bergschrund below the north face
waypoints.note: Cross the bergschrund at the base of Colfax's north face before the low-angle ice ramp; the schrund's character (snow bridge vs. open gap) varies season to season.

waypoints.name: Crux ice pillar (WI4)
waypoints.note: 30-40 ft near-vertical to slightly overhung water ice above the ramp; typically takes 5-6 screw placements.

waypoints.name: Colfax Peak
waypoints.note: True summit; descend toward the false (west) summit, around its south side to the Colfax-Baker saddle, then down the Coleman-Deming route.

gear: Ice screws for the crux pillar — about 40 ft of dead-vertical to slightly overhanging water ice, which fattens and eases later in the season
A few pitons — belays on the snow ramp between the ice steps are often pins rather than screws
Pickets for the snow gullies linking the ice
Crevasse rescue kit for the Coleman Glacier approach and the bergschrund at the start

road.name: Glacier Creek Road (FR 39)
road.status: Gravel, seasonal, and historically washout-prone. A 2021 washout at mile 3.8 was patched with a single-lane bypass reopened in November 2023, but December 2025 flood damage caused fresh washouts: as of June 30, 2026 the road is closed to all vehicles at the Glacier Creek bridge (MP 3.0) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead for repairs, expected to last through October 2026, though pedestrians, bikes, and e-bikes are allowed through at Forest Service discretion. Check current MBS NF alerts before you drive.
road.driveNote: From the Glacier Public Service Center in Glacier, WA, go east on the Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) about 1 mile to Forest Road 39 (Glacier Creek Road); turn right and follow FR 39 for 8 miles to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead (3,700 ft, parking on the left) -- note the road is currently closed to vehicles at MP 3.0, so budget extra time/distance to walk or bike in.
road.seasonalGate: Typically drivable late spring through fall; washouts, winter conditions, and the current 2026 repair closure can force a longer walk-in.

access.fees: Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead is a fee site: $5/vehicle/day or $30/year. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency (America the Beautiful) Pass, or the Recreation.gov digital pass all work; the WA Discover Pass is NOT accepted here.
access.rules: Pack out waste on the glaciers; Leave No Trace; group-size limits apply within the Mount Baker Wilderness.
access.permit: No climbing permit is required for Colfax Peak or Mt. Baker. A free self-issued wilderness permit is available at the trailhead register for day use -- fill it out and carry a copy.
access.closures: Glacier Creek Road (FR 39) has a history of washouts; December 2025 flood damage triggered a new closure to all vehicles at MP 3.0 (Glacier Creek bridge) to the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead starting June 30, 2026, expected through October 2026, with pedestrian/bike access allowed at Forest Service discretion -- check current Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts before driving.
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Wilderness), Mount Baker Ranger District
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker Ranger District) — Mount Baker Wilderness, with some upper routes crossing into North Cascades National Park
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at most trailheads — $30/year or $5/day.

overnight_permit.where: No climbing or wilderness permit. A recreation pass is needed to park at the Heliotrope Ridge and Park Butte trailheads; buy it ahead or on the Recreation.gov app.

road.name: Glacier Creek Road (FS-39)
road.status: Closed to vehicles at mile 3 for washout repairs (as of July 2026)
road.driveNote: From Glacier, WA on SR 542, turn onto Glacier Creek Road (FS-39) toward the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead; check current Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts before driving due to the active closure.
road.seasonalGate: Upper reaches typically snowed-in through winter/spring regardless of repair status

access.fees: $5 day-use fee or a valid Northwest Forest Pass / Interagency pass at the trailhead
access.closures: Glacier Creek Road (FS-39) closed to vehicles at mile 3 for washout repair as of July 2026 — verify current status with the Mt. Baker Ranger District before driving.
access.landManager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Ranger District (Mount Baker Wilderness)
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass (or interagency day-use pass)

overnight_permit.where: No climbing or wilderness permit. A recreation pass is needed to park at the Heliotrope Ridge and Park Butte trailheads; buy it ahead or on the Recreation.gov app.

before.descent: Most parties rappel/downclimb the route itself using V-thread anchors, reversing the bergschrund crossing; alternatively, traverse to the Colfax-Baker saddle and descend the standard Coleman-Deming route back to Hogsback Camp and the trailhead.

itinerary.cal: North-facing ice here is unusually reliable for the range (elevation, aspect, and geothermal heat keep it in) and can form as early as October, holding into May; the crux dagger pitch is condition-dependent and sometimes not fully formed.

days.note: Same approach as Cosley-Houston via Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman Glacier benches, but the route itself is harder and slower: a WI6 free-hanging ice dagger crux pitch adds real time, and most parties rappel/downclimb the route on V-threads rather than descending via the saddle, which also takes longer than a walk-off.
days.title: Car-to-car ascent

schedule.label: Leave Heliotrope Ridge trailhead
schedule.detail: Some parties car-camp at the TH; a couple reports describe 2:30-4:30am starts depending on party.

schedule.label: Reach the bench below Colfax (~6,600 ft)
schedule.detail: Rope up for glacier travel; stash poles/extra gear here.

schedule.label: Cross the bergschrund at the base of the north face
Begin climbing: AI4+ pitch, short snow slope, then the WI6 dagger crux
schedule.detail: The crux pitch is the pace-setter for the whole day.

schedule.label: Top out after mellow upper snow slopes
schedule.detail: Short traverse/scramble to the true summit.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Most parties rappel the route itself on V-thread anchors back to the bergschrund, then descend the standard Coleman-Deming route to the car.

days.objective: Summit Colfax Peak via the Polish Route and return to the trailhead same day

itinerary.totalNote: A long single day car-to-car from Heliotrope Ridge: roughly 12-13 hrs round trip with ~5,700 ft of gain/loss over ~9.0 miles, no camping — longer than Cosley-Houston mainly due to the WI6 crux pitch and a rappel descent of the route.

waypoints.name: Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Glacier Creek Road (FR 39), 8 mi from Hwy 542; Northwest Forest Pass required for parking, self-issue Mt. Baker Wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Climbers' Trail / Hogsback Ridge junction
waypoints.note: Fork just past the old Kulshan Cabin site; take the climbers' path right, up the Hogsback, toward the Coleman Glacier.

waypoints.name: Hogsback Camp
waypoints.note: Standard moraine-crest bivy at 6,000-6,200 ft used for both Coleman Glacier and Colfax north-face objectives.

waypoints.name: Coleman Glacier toward Colfax's north face
waypoints.note: Roped glacier travel across the Coleman toward the base of the face; watch for crevasses and serac fall from the icefall above.

waypoints.name: Bergschrund / mixed traverse
waypoints.note: Cross the bergschrund via a mixed rock-and-ice traverse to gain the base of the ice line, per route beta.

waypoints.name: Sustained AI4+ ice pitch
waypoints.note: A full ropelength of sustained steep ice leads up the line before the crux band.

waypoints.name: WI6 hanging ice curtain crux
waypoints.note: Free-hanging, rarely-formed ice dagger/curtain -- the route's defining pitch; only climbable in select conditions (formed only a handful of times per decade).

waypoints.name: Colfax Peak
waypoints.note: ~1,000 ft, 4-pitch line tops out near the true summit; descend via a series of V-thread rappels reversing the route, or traverse to the Colfax-Baker saddle.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: April through June, with April-May offering the firmest, most consistent ice

May.reason: Continuation of the firm spring window within the April-June best-season range

July.reason: The couloirs melt out in summer, increasing rockfall

June.reason: Rockfall and variable ice conditions once the route warms later in the season

April.reason: Firm alpine ice/snow on the Black Buttes couloirs as the prime season signature

March.reason: Couloir/ice line often not fully formed; thin or variable ice, which is more likely before the route is in full condition

weather.typical: Cold, firm conditions in the prime spring window; the route sits on the same exposed west shoulder of Mount Baker as Cosley-Houston and is subject to the same maritime storm cycles
weather.probability: Warming increases the rockfall hazard and can degrade the already-variable ice, reinforcing the value of the recommended 3-4 AM start

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High consequence: sustained, variable-condition steep ice above a bergschrund; harder and more sustained than the neighboring Cosley-Houston, raising the stakes of a fall or rockfall strike given the remote, technical-retreat setting

avalanche.zone: NWAC Mount Baker zone (covers the Black Buttes/Coleman Glacier approach)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Coleman Glacier approach involves roped glacier travel with crevasse hazard before reaching the bergschrund; the ice line itself is climbed above the bergschrund rather than on open glacier

road.name: Glacier Creek Road (FR 39)
road.status: Gravel, seasonal, and historically washout-prone. A 2021 washout at mile 3.8 was patched with a single-lane bypass reopened in November 2023, but December 2025 flood damage caused fresh washouts: December 2025 flood damage closed the road to all vehicles at the Glacier Creek bridge (MP 3.0) from June 2026; the Forest Service announced on 20 August 2026 that those repairs are complete and vehicles can again reach the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead. Check current MBS NF alerts before you drive.
road.driveNote: From the Glacier Public Service Center in Glacier, WA, go east on the Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) about 1 mile to Forest Road 39 (Glacier Creek Road); turn right and follow FR 39 for 8 miles to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead (3,700 ft, parking on the left). The MP 3.0 closure for flood repairs was lifted on 20 August 2026.
road.seasonalGate: Typically drivable late spring through fall; washouts, winter conditions, and the current 2026 repair closure can force a longer walk-in.
